s001.text: UPSC, twenty twenty-six. General Studies Paper Two, ten marks, a hundred and fifty words. Privacy and self-identity sit under Article twenty-one. Examine what the twenty twenty-six amendment did to the Transgender Persons Act. Here is the catch. The Act once gave a right to self-perceived identity. Did it survive?

s002.text: Read what it asks. Examine means weigh the effect and take a balanced view. There are three jobs. Set out the premise. Say what changed. Then test the effect against the right.

s003.text: Start with the premise. In twenty fourteen, in NALSA, the Supreme Court upheld a person's right to decide their own gender. In twenty seventeen, Puttaswamy quoted NALSA. Privacy, self-identity and autonomy are fundamental values.

s004.text: Puttaswamy also gave a yardstick. A law that invades privacy must pass three tests. Legality, a legitimate aim, and proportionality. Privacy is not absolute, but limits must be earned.

s005.text: But the twenty-nineteen Act went further. Section four, sub-section two gave a right to self-perceived gender identity. The twenty twenty-six Act, in section three, omits that sub-section. In force from the twenty-fifth of May.

s006.text: So identity now runs through a process. A medical board must recommend before the District Magistrate issues a certificate. The definition is a closed list. Its proviso excludes self-perceived sexual identities. The Act also adds heavier penalties for forcing a transgender identity.

s007.text: Now we write. A hundred and fifty words, about seven minutes. Open with the two judgments in one line. That sets the premise.

s008.text: Section one is what changed. Four short points. The omitted sub-section, the closed definition, the medical board, and the new penalties.

s009.text: Section two applies the three tests. Be careful with the last point. No court has ruled on this Act. So the verdict is a reasoned view, not a holding. It says the question awaits the courts.

s010.text: Now the easy answer beside it. It says self-perceived identity stays in section four. It does not. It says the Act began on assent. It began on a notified date. It says the Court struck it down. The record shows no ruling. And it never names the three-fold test.

s011.text: Here is the payoff. This one answer serves its cousins. Twenty seventeen asked about privacy as part of the right to life. Twenty twenty-three asked about gender justice. Learn the premise once.
